Saltwater care

Salt systems, maintained by people who actually like them.

Cell cleaning, output calibration, and corrosion checks — the upkeep salt pools quietly need.

Get a free quote Check if we cover your street
First, the honest bit

A saltwater pool is a chlorine pool.

It just makes its own. A salt cell runs a low-voltage current through salted water and splits it into chlorine on the spot, which sanitizes, does its job, and reverts to salt. That loop is why you're not hauling jugs home every fortnight — the salt is a reservoir, not a consumable.

So anyone selling you a "chlorine-free" pool is selling you a chlorine pool with better manners. What's genuinely different is the concentration: instead of a slug of chlorine once a week that spikes and fades, a cell trickles it in constantly. Steadier water, softer feel, no bleach smell on your skin.

The catch is that people hear "self-cleaning" and stop looking. A salt pool has more equipment than a chlorine pool, not less, and every piece of it is sitting in salted water. It needs less of your attention week to week and more of it every few months.

The short version

It's still chlorine
Same sanitizer, generated on site instead of poured in from a bottle.
Salt isn't used up
You top it up for rain, splash-out, and backwashing — not because the pool consumed it.
The cell does the work
And it's the one part with a service life. Treat it well and it lasts years; ignore it and it dies early.
pH climbs on its own
A quirk of the process. Salt pools need acid on a schedule, which surprises most new owners.
It still needs testing
A cell can be humming away and still be producing nothing. The test panel is the only thing that tells you.
Straight comparison

Salt or chlorine — which is actually better?

Neither, reliably. It depends on your pool, your surfaces, and how much you'd rather pay up front than weekly. Here's the trade honestly.

Saltwater

Gentler, steadier, more equipment.

  • Softer on skin, eyes, and hair — the difference is real, not marketing.
  • Chlorine arrives at a steady trickle instead of a weekly spike.
  • No jugs of chlorine in the shed, and no bleached swimsuits.
  • A cell to replace every few years — the real running cost.
  • Hard on natural stone coping, untreated aluminium, and cheap fittings.
  • Output drops off in cold water, so winter needs a hand.
vs
Chlorine

Simpler kit, more hands-on.

  • Nothing to break but the pump and filter. Fewer failure points, cheaper repairs.
  • Cheap to install, and it behaves the same in January as in July.
  • Easier to shock hard and fast when a pool goes sideways.
  • Chlorine gets bought, stored, and handled, forever.
  • Levels sawtooth between visits — high Monday, thin by Friday.
  • Stabilizer creeps up if you lean on tablets, and then nothing works.

We service both, and we'll tell you if the switch isn't worth it

If your pool is ringed in flagstone or you've got a heater with the wrong internals, converting to salt can cost you more in surfaces than it saves in chemicals. We'd rather say so before you spend the money than after.

What we do

Six things a salt pool needs from us.

The weekly clean is the same as any pool. This is the part that's specific to running salt.

Cell inspection and cleaning

The plates scale up with calcium and stop producing long before anything warns you. We pull the cell, look at it, and acid-wash it only when it needs it — routine acid baths shorten a cell's life as surely as neglect does.

Salt level testing

Most cells want somewhere around 2,700–3,400 ppm, depending on the maker. Too low and output falls away; too high and you're corroding fittings for no benefit. We test rather than guess, and add salt by the bag, not by the pinch.

Full water chemistry

pH, alkalinity, calcium hardness, and stabilizer — plus free chlorine, to prove the cell is actually doing what the display claims. Salt pools drift alkaline, so acid is a scheduled job here rather than an emergency one.

Filter cleaning and backwash

Salt pools throw fine particulate, and a loaded filter starves the cell of the flow it needs to work. We clean or backwash on pressure, not on the calendar — then top the salt back up, because backwashing takes some with it.

Skim, brush, and vacuum

Surface debris out, walls and steps brushed, floor vacuumed. Same as any pool — but brushing matters more here, because a steady low chlorine level is less forgiving of a film than a weekly shock is.

Corrosion and hardware checks

Ladder anchors, light rings, heater unions, sacrificial anodes, and the stone at the waterline. Salted splash finds every weak metal in a backyard, and it does it slowly enough that nobody notices until something is pitted.

Why bother

Salt pools fail quietly, and then expensively.

A chlorine pool tells you when it's unhappy — it goes cloudy, then green, and you deal with it. A salt pool with a scaled cell looks completely normal for weeks while its chlorine output slides toward nothing. By the time the water turns, you've usually lost the cell too.

That's the argument for regular service, and it's not a subtle one. Keeping the cell clean and the chemistry in range is the difference between replacing it on schedule and replacing it years early. The cell is the most expensive part of your pool, and calcium is what kills it.

The rest is the thing you actually bought the pool for: water that stays soft and clear without you thinking about it, and equipment that reaches the end of its service life instead of stopping halfway.

What we keep an eye on

Cell, every few months
Inspected on a cadence, cleaned when scale says so — not on a fixed date.
Salt, every visit
Rain and backwashing pull it down. A New Orleans summer of afternoon storms moves it more than you'd think.
pH, every visit
It climbs by design. Left alone, high pH scales the cell, which lowers output, which is how the spiral starts.
Winter output
Cells slow right down in cold water and mostly stop under about 60°F. We supplement through the cold snaps rather than pretend it's still working.
Stone and metal
Coping, anchors, anodes, heater internals. Caught early these are cheap; caught late they're a mason.
Before you book

Saltwater questions we get most.

How often should the salt cell be cleaned?

Inspected every three to six months, and cleaned only when there's scale on the plates. That's the important distinction — acid washing a clean cell strips plate coating and takes life off it, so "clean it every quarter regardless" is advice that costs you a cell. Our New Orleans tap water is hard enough that most cells here do need attention on the shorter end of that range.

Do saltwater pools still need chlorine?

They are chlorine — the cell just makes it instead of you pouring it. What you'll still buy occasionally is liquid chlorine for a cold snap, a heavy party weekend, or a post-storm shock, because a cell can't produce faster than its rated output no matter what the panel is set to.

Can saltwater damage my pool?

It can damage what's around your pool. The water itself is fine for plaster, tile, fiberglass, and vinyl at normal salt levels. Where it bites is natural stone coping, unsealed limestone and flagstone, untreated aluminium, and older heaters without the right internals — salted splash and evaporation leave crystals behind that work into the stone. Sealed surfaces, a sacrificial anode, and rinsing the deck handle nearly all of it.

Is a saltwater pool maintenance-free?

No, and that oversold promise is why we see so many neglected ones. It's lower-effort week to week — the chlorine handles itself — but it adds a cell, a control board, and a corrosion risk to the list of things that need looking at. Fewer trips to the store, more equipment to keep honest.

Can you convert my chlorine pool to salt?

Usually, yes, and we'll walk the deck with you first. The conversion itself is straightforward; whether it's a good idea depends on your coping, your heater, and how much you actually mind handling chlorine. We'll give you the real number and an honest recommendation, including "don't" if that's the answer.

My cell says it's working but the water's going off. What now?

That's the classic salt pool failure, and it's usually one of three things: scale on the plates, salt too low for the cell to run properly, or pH drifted high enough to blunt the chlorine that is being made. All three are diagnosable in one visit with a proper test panel — which is exactly what the panel on the wall can't tell you.
